title: NIST Cybersecurity Framework
summary: The NIST Cybersecurity Framework is a voluntary, outcome-based framework that organises cybersecurity activity into a common vocabulary so that technical teams, executives, auditors and regulators can discuss risk using the same terms. Its core is a set of Functions, historically Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, each broken into Categories and Subcategories that describe desired outcomes rather than prescribing specific products. Around that core sits the Framework Implementation Tiers, which characterise how rigorous and repeatable an organisation's risk management practice is, and the Framework Profiles, which express current and target states so a gap analysis produces a funded roadmap instead of a vague maturity claim. Practitioners use the framework in three concrete ways. First, as a mapping hub: an organisation maps its existing controls from ISO 27001, NIST SP 800-53, CIS Controls and regulatory obligations onto Subcategories once, then reuses that mapping for every new questionnaire. Second, as a reporting device: Function-level scores give executives a defensible view of capability without exposing implementation detail. Third, as a design input for metrics, where each Subcategory outcome gets an operational measurement such as mean time to detect or percentage of assets with current agent coverage. The framework is deliberately technology-neutral and does not itself create legal obligations, which is why it is frequently used as the connective tissue between mandatory regimes rather than as a replacement for them.
objectives: You will be able to describe the Functions, Categories and Subcategories and how they relate to Tiers and Profiles.
You will be able to build a current-state Profile from existing control evidence and a target Profile from business priorities.
You will be able to map ISO 27001, SP 800-53 and CIS Controls onto CSF Subcategories without duplicating effort.
You will be able to define operational metrics that demonstrate progress against Subcategory outcomes.
You will be able to explain to executives why a Tier rating is not the same thing as a maturity score or a certification.
You will be able to use the framework as the common language in a regulator or board conversation about residual risk.
